utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand? THE ACCUSED BRDJANIN: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ann Sutherland assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours I'm John Ackerman with Milan Trbojevic and Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, too. Can we proceed with the next witness or do you have further matters to thrash out?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour I wish to make an application for protective measures in relation to the next witness, BT-32. If we go into private session, I can give you the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand there is no objection on your part? Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There is no objection to going into private session if that's what you're asking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I mean. So we go into private session, Madam Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber, having heard submissions by Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution, requesting additional protective measures for Witness 7.204, consisting in particular to having his evidence tendered in closed session, in addition to the protective measures already granted, the Court -- the Chamber, upon considering that this witness has already been -- has already given evidence in the Stakic case and was granted this protective measure in that trial, for the same reasons and particularly those submitted by the Prosecution earlier on in private session, this Trial Chamber grants the application of the Prosecution and decrees that the testimony of the said witness be heard in closed session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Closed session, no? Closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. 25

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before we continue with the witness I've been passed a note to the effect that plenary in December has been cancelled and now the Stakic case is sitting from 9.00 a.m. until 1.00 p.m. -- I'm sorry, now the Stakic case is sitting from the 9th to the 13th of December and I had been asked if we are also sitting in the Brdjanin case from the 9th to the 13th of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Actually, as you know, Ms. Sutherland, I have just returned and I just have an idea of what is going on or is likely to go on, to happen. I haven't had time to discuss anything with Judge Schomburg except that I know that this is in the offing. I am on duty starting on the 13th of December, right through the 20th, and if it is okay with you, we can sit some of those days, if indeed the plenary dates, which had been set before, are cancelled, because I don't have yet a confirmation of that. There is a suggestion to have the plenary moved to the 2nd of December. Which brings me to something else I'll probably -- probably end of next week we will not be sitting because I need to travel. So the idea was to travel only on -- not be here Friday and Monday, but things are working in a way that probably we will have to miss the Thursday's sitting as well. I'm trying not to have that happen but I will be back to you as soon as my secretary has finalised the arrangements. So if we miss those two days perhaps we could find another two days but not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: The witness that's coming next week is a rather lengthy one and I don't know whether we will have examination and cross-examination in Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. So it may mean we reorganise and bring a shorter witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We can discuss that and I misspoke a moment ago, Your Honour, because we are sitting on the 9th and 10th of December already, so it will just be the 11th, 12th and 13th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think what I would suggest is this: I personally am tied up here until the 21st, so for me it doesn't really make a big difference but for my two colleagues it does because if they had arrangements already in place to travel upon the end of the plenary, then obviously it's not my intention to disrupt those plans so I think we need to have this discussed amongst ourselves first. If it is possible we will try to accommodate you. If it's not possible, of course, we will have to leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It seems as if it's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm very sorry I know I'm not robed but I was watching. Your Honour, it will cause the most incredible difficulties if we now have to change witnesses. The witness who is coming next week, who is arriving today, as Mr. Ackerman says, is a lengthy one, it may not be as lengthy as Mr. Ackerman anticipates but it will certainly be lengthy. In addition to that, in the week of the 6th -- 2nd of December, we have - I can't remember his number but - the military witness, about which Your Honour has heard a great deal, and on the 6th of December, fixed and 7.46, who is likely to take, well, I would think, I'm not sure, but I would certainly think three days, and on the 6th of December, Lord Ashdown has been fixed to testify and he's enormously difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can imagine that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: To get hold of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's go backwards again. 6th, you plan to have Lord Ashdown here?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We do. His staff have agreed that he will testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 6th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: From Monday to Wednesday, 7.46, the major military witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you plan to have that person testify from -- starting when?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On Monday, he's in full, Monday, the 2nd of December.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I won't be here. So Monday, I'm returning Monday. So if necessary, if we can find the time, we can sit for an extra hour or two on Tuesday and Wednesday, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, obviously we'll have to stop him, I think. We will have to try and sort that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My plans were to travel on Friday, but it seems that I won't be able to travel on Friday -- sorry, on Thursday evening which wouldn't have disrupted anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's next Thursday, Your Honour is talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly, tomorrow week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That would enable us, I'm pretty certain, to finish 7.46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What happened was this, that for reasons that I don't understand, my secretary has been informed that on that day, the time I was supposed to land or -- the airport will be closed for three hours or four hours and it doesn't make sense to me, because as an alternative, they suggested another flight which would still get me the same airport at a time when supposedly it would be closed, so I'm still not understanding anything. However, I asked her to check properly and she should be in a position to confirm everything tomorrow morning. Alternatively, in order not to miss the Thursday sitting, I suggested to her to see other alternatives, what other alternatives there could be. Which I'm pretty sure aren't many because of the location where I need to travel. But any way, by tomorrow this time I should know precisely what the arrangements are and then we can -- I'm trying to reduce it as much as possible, and if it is necessary, absolutely necessary, then perhaps I would try to return Sunday rather than Monday, but I have to chair a meeting and I think the meeting that I have to chair is on Monday. This is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's next Monday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The 2nd. Now it seems that the plenary is being moved to Monday, the 2nd as well so in any case, if -- indeed, if it is moved to 2nd, 3rd of December, that would mean that there would be no sittings on the 2nd and the 3rd of December.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I know Your Honour feels that we sometimes make difficulties about this question of changing witnesses but, Your Honour, it really is -- particularly for the Defence who rightly need to know in advance and if we are suddenly changing because I don't know there has been a change in the dates of the plenary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I actually got informed of the suggestion, it's a suggestion that is being made, to have the dates originally scheduled for -- fixed for the plenary, I think 11, 12, 13th of December, cancelled, and have the 2nd, 3rd and 4th of December instead, I have only discussed it very briefly with one of my colleagues who gave me the information. I haven't seen the document as yet because my secretary has still got them. I meant to go through everything between today and tomorrow, and then see what the situation is, because I realise that if we don't sit on the 2nd, 3rd and 4th of December because of the plenary, that's going to cause some serious disruption of our timetable and as I said, I mean, I personally would have no problems sitting the 11th, 12th and 13th of December but if those days are -- will be available and the courtroom will be available, but I don't know what the other two judges' arrangements are for their Christmas holidays so I still have to discuss it with them and I don't think this is the place where we should discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I imagine Mr. Ackerman, like most of us I think, we've all made plans on the base that is the 10th was the last day of sitting but it's not so desperate in our case because we can arrange witnesses for people we know are going to be here to call, although because the Stakic Defence case is running as well, it's causing a certain amount of juggling, we have had to alter the witnesses but can I ask this, perhaps, Your Honour? It really is important because if we have to change the witnesses round, and we need to know as soon as possible which days we are sitting and which we are not. So perhaps if we could be told tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'll try and do my best to get all the information. In the meantime, I had in mind also, this is happening I'm just thinking aloud at the moment, if it will be all right with the other two judges and of course with you, if that particular week of December we could sit right through the 13th, then it was my intention to suggest to you that in January, instead of starting on the 6th or the 7th - because it was my intention to honour the Orthodox Christmas or at least - we could have the entire of that week off and then start on the 11th, but I would ask you to sit at least until the 13th of December. In other words you will have a whole week off, extra week off in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd ask very strongly that even if we don't sit the 6th and the 7th because of the Orthodox Christmas, that's Monday and Tuesday, we do start on the Wednesday. I'm getting really concerned about the delay in this case. We said we'd try and finish our case by Easter and that seems to be a proper cutoff point but if we are losing all these days in December and we are going to lose more in January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the way it seems that the first week of December is going to be disrupted, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's for sure. And if -- I've seen a document, I've been shown a document, by one of my colleagues suggesting the 2nd, 3rd and 4th of December as alternatives for the plenary. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't like to ask because of course it's a matter for the judges but unless there is a very good reason, is there -- why the plenary can't stick to its original dates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There seems to be a good reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, excuse me, but could it be slowed down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, I'll come back to you tomorrow, in the meantime do try and cultivate the idea of working an extra couple of days in the second week of December and then taking off the days I suggested in January.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think Mr. Ackerman --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's hear what Mr. Ackerman has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is just enormously disruptive to publish a schedule, to allow people to make plans based upon that schedule, and then to say, "Sorry, we are going to change it." For a long time now I have had plans that were made based upon the 10th being our last day of sitting in December. Family plans, business plans. I desperately need to be in the United States and be able to fly there on the 11th of December. I have a ticket. The plans are made. I understand the problems we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, let me interrupt you for a second. Perhaps we could identify a witness that Mr. Trbojevic could handle those two days, or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That may be possible, Your Honour. The problem is that we are in the Prijedor phase and we are dealing with transcripts that are only in English but there may be a way to get around that. That's a possibility. And I'll certainly look into that. But I wish we would adopt a policy that once we decide what days we are going to sit, that those are the days we are going to sit, and not decide at the last minute that, "gee, there's a court open on Friday let's sit on Friday," because we really do make plans in advance based upon that calendar and those plans may involve some intensive work on the case to be prepared to do something different. It's not that we go off and party and carouse and things like that it's that we work on those days off. I have not had a day off since I can't remember when. I've worked every day for a long time. I'm not asking for a medal again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You won't get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I know I won't get it but that's what's going on. And I just wish we could stay with the days. While I'm on my feet, can I raise another matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I was handed as I came into the courtroom today, it's about a 70 page, as near as I can tell, transcript of what I was told was Rule 68 material regarding the witness that's about to come in and start testifying. I would request, as a result of that, that I not be required to cross-examine that witness until tomorrow when I've had a chance to go through this new material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that all right with you, Ms. Sutherland? I know you have two witnesses in the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have another witness to testify after this witness. Just in relation to what Mr. Ackerman just said, the 70 odd pages is of a transcript of a witness who testified in another case. There is, in fact only three pages that relate -- which is the potential Rule 68 in relation to this next witness. I will hand Mr. Ackerman a note which gives him the exact page numbers that he can go to, but I agree if he wants to put the cross-examination off until tomorrow that's fine by me. But once he reads these pages he may not wish to put the cross-examination off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I've taken note of your submission and request. And also of the non-objection on the part of the Prosecution should it be the case. Mr. Ackerman, when you are in a position to either confirm your request or change it, you will let us know, all right? In the meantime, if it is necessary to have the witness cross-examined tomorrow, then obviously, there being no objection, you will cross-examine the witness tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, for everyone's benefit, Your Honour, the order of witnesses for this week just so everyone is clear, and Mr. Ackerman is being very accommodating because we've changed the order a number of times to accommodate counsel who are involved in other cases, at the moment, the order is that the first witness is 7.204, the second witness will be 7.225, the third witness will be 7.79 and the final witness for this week will be 7.226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So I think we need to go into closed session now, correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There being no further submissions, we go into closed session, and bring in Witness BT-28?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour as I understand the agreement that was made between the parties was that for these Prijedor witnesses who have previously testified, Your Honours have their transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. What we don't know is if Mr. Ackerman has received a replica of our bundle as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: So I will not -- the agreement as I understand it is I will not lead the witness live through his rather remarkable story except to perhaps touch on areas that he did not or that I failed to ask him the first time and then that Mr. Ackerman will cross-examine him; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, any additional information or confirmation or -- any way, it's the usual procedure that is adopted in other trials as well when this takes place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I was just wondering if there would be a conflict of interest if I got Mr. Ackerman to negotiate my contract with the UN next time because I think he made a pretty good deal on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you can bring the witness in, please, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Incidentally, Mr. Ackerman, perhaps we can go through just I want to make sure what you have and what you don't have. Maybe you have another 70 pages. What we have been given is a map of Kozarac and Omarska overview which is P1146. Then we have exhibits from Stakic, S51 which is the usual map surrounded by photos. Then a -- two photos, S15/26 and S15/29. Then witness statement to the Prosecutor, to the investigator, sorry, of the Tribunal dated 11th January, 1996. And then some other -- and then the transcript of the testimony -- it's okay, it's okay, -- which starts from page 6372 -- sorry, 6326. I think we have some missing here. There must be some mistake because mine starts at 6326, stops at 6361, and then recommences at 6372. But it could well be -- yeah, no, no, it's okay. It doesn't make a difference because basically the witness entered court so there must be a number of pages relating to some other matter we are not interested in. So the second part of the testimony of the witness starts on page 6372 in the Stakic transcript. And this is the sitting of the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Shall I proceed? Is everyone ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the short answer is I don't have the packet that was handed to you. Now, whether I can assemble all those things that were given to me over the last several weeks, I probably could. I don't know until I see what was given to you I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you been given the transcript of his testimony in Stakic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Absolutely, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's basically what we have. The rest are the statement that is he gave, the statement he released, gave to the investigator of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I've got all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then it's two photos plus a map so I wouldn't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm quite certain I have the photos and the map somewhere. I was just getting ready to look. I thought I'd prepared them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If there is a problem we'll stop for the time being. So Mr. Poljak, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand this is not the first time you are giving evidence in a trial because you have already testified in the Stakic case. So I will cut my introduction short. You are about to give evidence in this case. It will be much shorter than the one you gave in Stakic because we have a transcript of all your testimony, your entire testimony, in the other case, and we will be making use of it in this case. So you will only be asked a few questions in addition to what is already contained in that transcript. As you know, and I'm sure you're familiar with this, before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you enter a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony, you will be telling us the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. The usher is going to hand you now the text of the solemn declaration and I would now invite you to read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking to this Tribunal that you will testify the truth. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down and Mr. Koumjian for the Prosecution will be directing a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps the exhibit previously marked in this case as P1146 could be put on the ELMO? I'll be referring to it shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please. Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Poljak. Can you tell the Court which has your transcript, and has read your transcript, just to remind us of a few things, you talked in the transcript about being at home the day that Kozarac was attacked on the 24th of May, 1992. How old were you at that time?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I was 19, 19 and one month to be exact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you live with at that time? Who was in the home where you were living?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I was living in a house with my parents and my middle brother lived with us there. He was married so that his wife also lived with us in our family house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did his wife have a child? Did you have a nephew or niece?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, she did have and she does have the child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was the child in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: About six months, an infant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us on the map that's in front of us the area that you lived in, the house, your parents' house, where you were on the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I can do it only approximately. I think that it's here more or less.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And for the record you're pointing to an area between what's marked G or Gornji Jakupovici or D or Donji Jakupovici; is that correct? You lived in between Gornji and Donji Jakupovici, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your prior transcript were you asked quite a bit on cross-examination about the checkpoint in Jakupovici. Can you point on the diagram to where that checkpoint was?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was on the main Prijedor-Banja Luka road, over here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're indicating the road that runs closest to Donji Jakupovici. Can you describe, physically describe, what that checkpoint looked like, what you called a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what it exactly looked like. Some logs had been brought to the road but I did not see it. This was made -- put up two or three days before the attack, something like that, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You described -- before we go to the attack, did you yourself have any military training? Did you ever serve in the JNA or in any other military or paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No. I didn't serve in the army. I wasn't a member of any unit. I was going to school in Prijedor. I was completing the final fourth year of the mechanical technical school in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked in your transcript you talk about what happened to you and your family during the attack on Kozarac. There is -- there has been allegations made by some individuals or statements made that the attack on Kozarac began because a convoy of the JNA was attacked at Jakupovici at that checkpoint. What do you know about that? When I say the JNA I mean the JNA or former JNA, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were not present at the checkpoint when the attack -- any time the day of the attack on Kozarac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. Neither that day or the day before. I don't know if I was ever there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the attack on Kozarac came, you talked in the transcript about running to various locations and there being shelling. Can you tell me the direction that the shelling came from?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I had the feeling that the shells were coming from all directions. When you heard the first shot, it wasn't a shot, it was like a very large fireworks display. There was shooting on all sides. So it was impossible to tell from which direction it was coming from. It was frightening. You could hear very loud explosions, you could hear the firing from regular weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack happening on the Sunday, the 24th, had you seen the army, the VRS, the former JNA, making any preparations in the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: This went on for a while. We watched this for a while, military vehicles, at night you could hear, according to the estimates of the people from the village that -- they could hear tanks, powerful sound of engines, the children who went to elementary school at Lamovita saw that there were many soldiers stationed there as well as weapons, quite sometime before the attack on Kozarac was carried out. I also saw, myself, on a hill called Cuklac which is not far from my house, there we could see soldiers digging in the artillery, the mortars, Howitzers and so on. It took a while but even though nobody believed that the attack on Kozarac would actually be carried out, there was no reason for it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Realising that you were not, yourself, at the checkpoint did you ever hear anyone who was at the checkpoint, did anyone who was present ever tell you what occurred between the army and the people at the checkpoint that started the firing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I object to that unless he can -- unless he can identify who it was that told him what he heard, if anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What do you have to say about the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'd certainly ask him to identify to the best of his ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So ask that question rather than the one you asked before, because the objection raised by Mr. Ackerman is being sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present that told you about what happened at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: My cousin, who is no longer with us, Sakib Poljak, he told me about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And since Sakib Poljak cannot tell us about what happened -- by the way, why is it that Sakib Poljak isn't here to tell us about what happened?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He cannot tell us about it because like the majority of the population of Kozarac, he was detained in a camp, just like that, he and myself and thousands of others were in Omarska. He was beaten day after day. He was taken from Omarska. He was killed. We don't know what happened to him but all traces of him are lost from Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is not responsive to the question, Your Honour. It's a story that's being told about his cousin now that he can only know from hearing from someone else, I'm sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he's explaining actually -- I think he's answering the question because the question was, and "since Sakib Poljak cannot tell us about what happen -- by the way why is it that Sakib Poljak isn't here to tell us about what happened." He could have answered because he hasn't been summoned, because he didn't want to, he's explaining.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He's deceased.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object then to his giving any evidence about that because there is no way we can independently verify it. We certainly can't call the cousin as a witness or speak to the cousin and therefore it is just pure hearsay and there is no one around for us to confront in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But your objection is still not being sustained, the reason being is that he is explaining why is it that he is not here to give evidence. He is giving his own version.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm objecting to him giving the answer to the next question which is: "What did Sakib tell you?" I'm objecting to that because there is no way I can independently verify that. No one for me to confront as a witness to that event and therefore I think it's improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It will be admitted just the same, Mr. Ackerman, but of course the position will be that the fact that the witness is not here or the person is not here and can't possibly be here to be examined or cross-examined will be taken into consideration but he is no different than any other person that has been referred to as having given -- passed on information and who is now dead. We've had several of them. Yes, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak, the Defence counsel asked if there is any way for to you know that your cousin was detained in Omarska and that he disappeared from Omarska and was beaten there. Is there way to know that, can you help him, how you learned that information?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We were staying in adjacent rooms when I was in Omarska, so that I had the opportunity a couple of times to go from my room to that room to see how they are and to talk to them during the time that they were alive in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say, "They," are you talking about Sakib and someone else? Can you tell us who the other person is?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I'm thinking of Sakib, Saban, Sabit. They are my cousins, my relatives. I'm thinking of my uncle Jusuf, he survived. I'm thinking of my neighbours who were also in that same room, Husein, Bilal, I'm thinking of Nihad Jakupovic. I'm thinking of the three brothers, Jusuf, Kasim and Garo who are no longer with us. Many neighbours, who were beaten, tortured, interrogated, robbed and finally all traces of them are lost. They were taken away, killed, I don't know what happened to them. And my own father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did Sakib tell you about what happened -- first of all, did he tell you that he was at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did he tell you happened at the checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The conversation I had with him about what happened at the checkpoint took place when we were fleeing the village. It was just a short conversation about what happened, and he told me that at one point, a tank came from the direction of Banja Luka, and a large number of soldiers suddenly split up behind the tank on each side of the Prijedor-Banja Luka road. They had automatic rifles and they started firing. So when the shooting occurred or when the shooting started, they escaped, they fled from there so there wasn't really that much to talk about. The situation was such that we were, how shall I put it, we were frightened, we were out of our minds with fear, we were escaping. It wasn't a situation where people could actually sit down and talk about what happened. We were running. It was very uncertain. A person didn't know what was ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've talked about that flight and being captured eventually, separating from your family, saying goodbye to your mother and father, your sister-in-law and the child and that while they went into Prijedor, you went over the mountains trying to walk to Croatia and you were captured and taken to Benkovac barracks. I know you have many things that happened during that journey. The judges have it in the transcript so I'm not going to go over all that happened to you during that journey. But at Benkovac barracks, you mentioned a hodza. Can you tell us again the name of that hodza or how you -- how you knew him?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: His name was Hamid Softic. I think his last name is Softic. I'm not sure about his last name. His name was Hamid. Everybody knew him. I knew him. He worked, he was on duty for a while in the mosque at Gornji Jakupovici, when I was still little; maybe I was seven, eight or ten years old. Then, most recently, he worked at the Kamicani mosque. He was married to a woman from Jakupovici so I knew him fairly well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about at Benkovac various people being beaten but when you were detained in the bathroom and that he was called out many times; is that correct, the hodza?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why he was targeted or called out more than other people?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I don't know, probably because he was a hodza.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about seeing his upper body when he was sitting on a chair, being black and blue. I think in your testimony in Stakic, that was the last time you talked about seeing this hodza. Did you ever see the hodza again after you were transferred to the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He was transferred together with me and the others to Omarska, to the garage, but I don't know, I think that immediately, the next day, a man whom I don't know, who was at Benkovac and who probably took part in the torture of Hamid, the hodza, came, like I said I don't know whether that was the very next day or a day or two later, but any way, he came one morning, called out the hodza, and said, "You are coming with me." And he took him away. He came on a motorcycle. I don't know what he did, where he went, but all traces of Hamid the hodza are lost from that point on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You then discussed in your testimony the garage where you were kept when you were first taken to Omarska. So that we can have some kind of picture in our minds of that place, can you point to some areas in this courtroom and tell us approximately the dimensions of the garage? Was it as big as this room or a portion of this room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was much smaller than this room. It was maybe four by four metres, maybe the height of the room was 2 -- 20 metres. It was as wide as a regular garage door, and then another normal door.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men were put in the garage with you when you first arrived at Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I am not sure about the number of people because there are many numbers running through my head. 100, 150, these numbers seem to be coming again and again, about 100, 150 people were transferred from Benkovac to Omarska. The same number approximately remained at Omarska after all the other people who were detained at Omarska and who survived were transferred to Manjaca and Trnopolje. Also that was about the number of the people, the last persons who remained at Omarska. The same number was transferred from Manjaca to Batkovici so I'm not sure about the numbers. These numbers are repeated very often. 100 to 150 people approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Recognising it's very hard to estimate numbers, can you describe the proximity that you were in with the other people? How close were you? Did you have an arm between you? Were you able to lie down? Can you describe the conditions in that garage?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The first evening, the first two or three evenings, there was no room even to turn around. We were all standing up. The first two or three days, no one sat down. You couldn't. There was no room. There was no air. And then I don't know after how many days they started to take people away. I remember very well, there were people -- I mean these people were -- their last name was Garibovic there were five or ten of them, so all of them were taken away from that group in the garage. I myself after ten days was take be away and interrogated. The worst time was during the first four or five days. I don't know, I'm not sure, you couldn't even turn around, there was no room. We were standing up the whole time. It was like in a gas chamber, there was no air to breathe. We -- for three days, we didn't. We were brought in on Friday, then we were there Saturday. On Sunday, they gave us this sack with some bread in it to eat. It's very difficult to explain, to describe this. It was just terrible. It was impossible. It's impossible to describe. It was hell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified it was very hot. Can you give us any estimate of the temperature in Centigrade or can you in any other way describe to the Judges how the heat felt and how it affected the people in that garage?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: When they put us into that garage and after they closed the door, it wasn't long afterwards that because there was such a big crowd of people in such a small space, that the temperature soared. It was very hot. The walls were painted by just -- with normal paint which in some ways started to melt and I remember very well they would give us canisters of water and they brought that in through the windows, and then there would be a crowd there around that window. There would be a struggle to get to that water, to drink, to survive. So that the -- there was a lot of pressure, and I remember very well, I put my hand on the wall, and the paint started to rub off. It was melting down. And there were also drops from the condensation which were falling from the ceiling. It was just terrible. But the worst thing was with the air. You couldn't breathe. We were practically suffocating.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone pass out or have any effect from that condition, the first night or two days that you were in the garage?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The first night, I think two men of about 30 or 35 years of age died. They died. They suffocated. I don't know what happened to them. They weren't beaten or anything. They were there together with us. In any case, I remember that they died. Then there were five or six cases of people who, how shall I put it, just went crazy. They went mad. They were not aware of where they actually were. They thought that they were somewhere else. I remember one man, he was a younger man, he was maybe about my age, he started to hallucinate: "Get out of that forest, what are you doing there? The Chetniks are coming. They will kill us." There was another elderly man who was looking into my eyes as if he were looking through me. He started to talk to me, "Come on, young man, saddle the horses. We are going." It was very strange. It's very difficult to describe the situation. Then the entire time, the first night when we got there, when they locked us up, they forced us to sing songs. They shouted from the other side, "Tomorrow we are bringing your mothers and your sisters to rape them and you can watch." And things of that kind. I have no idea how I survived and how it is that I'm still normal, if I am normal. I really don't know. It was really terrible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What opportunities did you have to use the -- to go to the bathroom when you were in the garage for the ten days?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: During the day, they let us outside occasionally to go to the toilet, and even though a person avoided going to the toilet out of fear, I don't remember whether it was the first or the second day that I went out of that garage for the first time, it was morning. They allowed me to go about ten metres away from the entrance to the garage to pee. I remember that feeling very well, when I came out. It was sunny, it was May, the weather was nice. Maybe it was about 10.00 or 11.00 in the morning. Three or four metres away from me was the body of one of the men who had suffocated on the first or the second day, I think, in that garage. I went outside and I wasn't even paying attention to that. There was a dead man lying there. It didn't even prompt any kind of feelings in me. It was as if it was just a piece of wood, a log, a rock. The things that did elicit any kind of feelings from me was the fact that I was out in the fresh air, in the sun, that I was out of the garage for the first time in two or three days, one or two days, and that I could breathe in fresh air. It was a totally abnormal situation. It was awful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know that man who had suffocated, whose body you saw?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He was older than I. I know that he came from Kamicani but I can't remember his name now, and the other one, who suffocated too to death, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that bread was brought a few days after you arrived in Omarska. Was that the first time you were fed in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. The first time that this group arrived with which I was, we arrived there on Friday evening or late afternoon, and at some time on Sunday afternoon, they opened the door and threw in bread in a paper bag, so of course everybody was trying to get to this bread because there wasn't enough of it. I remember I managed somehow to get two slices of bread.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the two slices of bread that you were able to fight for?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: One slice, I put in my pocket. You could say that I hid it in my pocket. And the other one, I ate slowly, crumb by crumb. How shall I put this? I mean, it's -- it beggars the imagination. It was at some animal level, it wasn't human. There was nothing human about the situation that we were in. The only thing that mattered -- I mean instinct reigned, not mind. The water canister was put in through the window and I never even thought: "How shall I get to this canister and have some water." You simply fought for it. As when you throw a bone, a piece of meat, to dogs and then they start fighting over it. That is how we behaved too. There was nothing, you are younger, you are stronger, you are older, you are weaker, nothing mattered. The only thing that mattered was to somehow get at that bread or get at that water. I mean it was simply some instincts which all of a sudden had taken complete sway.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there someone in the garage who you knew, a neighbour named Enes, who was sick?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That's right. He wasn't my neighbour. He came from Kamicani but his sister was married to a neighbour of mine. Yes. Enes, his father, I think there were some relatives. Whether it was that day when they gave us this bread, I think that that day he felt very bad, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned -- you mentioned eating one piece of bread and you said you saved the other in your pocket. What happened to that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Since I knew his father, and him, I knew them well, I mean the family, his father was also a bricklayer and he was building our new house when my family were building the house when I was small so that I knew them and his sister was married to my neighbour, and so that I was sitting or crouching or whatever, squatting there, and I could see that he was not feeling well and I was thinking what to do, whether to give, whether to take out this slice of bread and give it to him, that is to give them, to give him, perhaps, it might help him, or to keep it for myself, and finally I decided to give them this piece of bread that I had with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you present the day that the -- I want to move now on to a different subject -- to August of 1992. You're aware now that a few journalists, one of them Penny Marshall, came to the Omarska camp in early August, 1992. You're aware of that now?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I know that journalists came but who those journalists were, where they had come from, I have no idea. Yes, there were journalists, most of them came at a time when only 150 of us were left in Omarska but before that, I know there was a delegation, there was a group of journalists who came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know the answer to this. You tell me. Have you ever seen videotape of journalists who first came to Omarska and videotaped only in the cafeteria some prisoners going to -- for the soup and bread in the cafeteria? Were you present in that cafeteria the time the journalists first came?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. I was in Omarska. I was at the Omarska camp at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But is it correct that you were not one of the people that went to the cafeteria and are on that first videotape? Let me --

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, no. I wasn't, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see, while you were at Omarska, any foreigners or foreign journalists come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I did not -- I could not see them to begin with I was in the garage and during that time nobody came and besides you couldn't see anything from there. And then they transferred me to another room in the bigger hangar where the dumptrucks were and from there you couldn't see anything either. And journalists did not come to that particular room, not at least to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In August of 1992, did some foreigners come and did conditions change in Omarska?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: About 150 of us - well those 150 again - were kept in Omarska. I didn't know it at the time. It was other people were taken by buses from Omarska, we didn't know where, until the day when the Red Cross registered us and until they told us that some people had been transferred to Trnopolje, or to Manjaca, and that they had also been registered by the Red Cross and 150 of us were kept there in Omarska and that day, when we stayed there, we had somehow accepted our fate, that they would kill us, and we were very much afraid. But it was pretty quiet. Nobody came to tease us to provoke us, the guards didn't come, nothing so we didn't really know what was in the offing and what would happen to us. And late at night about 2.00 or 3.00 in the morning, we heard trucks, and the guards came then and ordered us to come out and to unload whatever was in those trucks, and those were beds with bed linen. We were completely at a loss. We didn't know what was going on. But we took it all to a room which was in the same building as the garage, in which I was put up first. So we lined those beds in there and the bed linen, and in matter of fact those beds were meant for us so that after three months, I had for the first time the opportunity to lie in a bed. The conditions changed completely. There was no more mistreatment. It meant the food got better They even procured shaving appliances and there was also a barber with us, a male hair dresser who started looking after us, that is, cutting our hair. We were also issued with some hygiene articles so we did not know what was going on. We were at a loss. What was that all about? And that went on for I don't know how many days. We also went all over the camp, cleaning, WCs, and traces of torture and killing. I know that a couple of guys went to remove several dead bodies, not far from the camp, which had lain there for a long time and I remember it well. It stuck in my memory. When they tried to move them, they simply -- these bodies, I mean they simply disintegrated. The arm came off, a leg came off. So that is what we did for a few days. And then journalists started coming. I don't know who was the first to come, whether it was the Red Cross or journalists. But we then began to have visitors almost every day, foreign journalists, the Red Cross, who registered us. So we began slowly to get some information about what was going on elsewhere in Bosnia, and we began to hope that we might survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the council, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There is one photograph that apparently that's not in evidence. It has the ERN number 02123687.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Could this be shown to the witness? Did Your Honour want -- I'm not familiar any more with the procedures do we premark it? Do we give it an exhibit number now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I suggest we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May that be P1128.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Poljak do you recognise anything in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, beds looked like these here and this room does remind me of the room that I was kept in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the visit of the foreigners, this is what the room looked like after the foreigners visited and the beds were brought in?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, the room was furnished before the journalists and the Red Cross came. That day when others were taken to Manjaca. I mean in the evening, at night, a truck came, as I've just told you, at 3 o'clock in the morning and that is when we furnished those rooms and after we put it all in order, three or four days later, journalists started to come but we had already put this room in order. There was bed linen in place and everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned your father and you testified in your -- in the Stakic case that you said goodbye to your father when you decided to try to make your way to Croatia and he stayed with your -- with your sister-in-law and her child and your mother, and you also testified you saw him again in Omarska. Were you in the same room in Omarska at any point?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: When some ten days later I was taken from interrogation from the garage, they transferred me after the interrogation to the same room where my father was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was your father? What was his occupation before the attack on Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He worked for a long time as a bricklayer in Croatia, the company was called Pula Siporeks. Then he also worked privately at Suma, that is, many members of my family were engaged in forestry business so that he had spent a large part of his life doing that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he politically active or did he -- was he militarily active? Was he part of any paramilitary group?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Politically, no, he was not politically active. And he was not with any military formation either, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your father was called out many times and beaten. Do you know why?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: He reluctantly spoke about that, and when I asked him: "Well what was it, how was it," his usual answer would be, "It's all right, it's okay, never mind, they just hit me slightly." I suppose they didn't want me, they didn't want me to worry about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified your father was called out one night and never returned. Does it bother you that to this day you don't know where your father's body is?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Judges why?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, it's very simple. I mean the mere thought, you know, when you lose one of your loved ones, then you bury those persons, you do whatever is due on such occasions. You know he or she is dead, so we shall bury this person, we shall bring flowers. We shall honour the person's memory. I don't know how my father was killed and I'm practically 100 per cent sure that he was killed, that he's dead, that he's no more. Was he tortured? How did they kill him? Was it a rifle? I'd be the happiest if that was the case, or axes which they also did, hammers, all sorts of objects. So that is -- that is a question that troubles me. Where do his bones lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Mr. Ackerman? Can I ask you how long you anticipate your cross will take? The idea is to see whether we should break now for 15 minutes or so or in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Probably about the same as the last witness, Your Honour. I think that was 20, 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we can go ahead. We can go ahead. Do you have another witness today?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So interpreters and technicians, shall we proceed until we finish? We anticipate we are talking of another 25 minutes or so and then it will be over for the day.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'm told I made another mistake. Your Honour, may the package of Mr. Poljak's testimony in the Stakic case be entered into evidence as P1521?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1521, all right. Yes, Mr. Ackerman. This last photo that you showed the witness, you haven't given to us. We don't have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in the bundle of photographs, the big bundle of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Poljak.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to testifying in the Stakic case, you've given a few statements. You gave one to the Office of the Prosecutor in January of 1996, correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that statement that you gave to the Prosecutor -- and if you want to look at it, just let me know and I'll see that you get one to look at -- I'm reading from the English here on page 2 of the statement, numbered page 2, it's actually the first page of the English statement. You say, "I think that about" -- you're talking about after the attack on your village and what happened, and how you left Kozarac and then got captured. "We were captured on 27 May, 1992. I think that about 80 people all together were captured. Some of them armed and dressed in uniforms." How many would you say were dressed in uniforms of that 80?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Several of them, four, five men perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Four or five? How many were armed?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I wouldn't know exactly. Afterwards, I was taken to collect those weapons and there were several automatic rifles, some hunting weapons, some ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many weapons would you say that you collected? There were three of you collecting weapons of the -- between the three of you, how many weapons did you collect?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know exactly because at that moment, it -- I never gave it a thought how many weapons, why I did that, all I was thinking about was what would happen to me and I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened was when it became clear that you were all going to be captured you dropped your weapons there in the woods, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You didn't have a light submachine-gun? I'm saying you didn't have a light submachine-gun?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I didn't. I didn't have a single weapon, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your best estimate that you can give us today of how many weapons, automatic weapons, rifles, whatever, that you collected, the three of you, there in the woods that day?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Ten, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else collected weapons from the woods besides the three of you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: We were escorted by a guard who belonged -- I suppose -- to the reserve force. He had the old olive green-grey army uniform, and then there were some soldiers who were deployed in the woods. I suppose as guards, wearing camouflage uniforms with red berets, as far as I can remember, and there was the soldiers who came with us and talked and took us to collect those weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those -- the 80 of you that had left Kozarac and went into the woods, you really were -- you were all part of an organisation that was armed and trying to defend Kozarac, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That is not so. I was at Brdjani in the basement, like I explained to you, when the decision came down for the people to surrender to the army, to the Serb authorities, I and my sister-in-law's brother decided not to go and to go to the woods and to try to cross over into Croatia. That's when I said goodbye to my parents, to my father and my mother, and we set out towards the woods. We -- there were not 70 armed men with us. There was only two of us. He was grown up. He was older. He knew the terrain and our plan was to cross over into Croatia, not to get killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1075, please? Oh, I'm sorry, forget it. Don't talk to me any more, okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When the microphone is on, you can hear that stuff, can't you? Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There came a time, sir, at Omarska, and were you asked about this on direct, by Mr. Koumjian, when the foreign journalists came to the camp and I'm talking about before people left and went to Trnopolje and Manjaca, and it was that -- that time that you said you weren't aware, at the time they were there, that they were in fact there, correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I knew about the Trnopolje camp but I didn't know that this other group had been taken to Manjaca. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question it's probably because I didn't phrase it very well. At the time the foreign journalists were at Omarska, when everyone was there, you didn't know that they were there. The day they were there, you weren't aware of their presence?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: When the first group of journalists came, at the point in time when they did come, I didn't know, but perhaps already the next day, there was talk about them having been there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And you knew that because you heard from other people about the fact that they had been there, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say this is a true statement: Any one in Omarska would know very soon about anything that happened there because news travelled fast in Omarska? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They travelled fast, yeah. This is what I found out. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for instance, you learned even though you weren't out on the pista, you learned from other people things that were happening out on the pista, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything exactly that I remember 100 per cent. That's something that I cannot do. I don't remember everything. This wasn't something very important that I troubled myself to remember or to think about. I heard this from information that was going around. I don't know who I heard it from, how I heard it from -- how I heard it. I don't know. The conditions were so terrible in the camp, psychologically that a person clung to straws. It's possible that I heard about the journalists later also. I don't know when I heard about it but I did hear about it. Those journalists did come but I didn't know about it when they just came, that first group. I don't know what you would like me to say about it, for me to tell you in detail about when the journalists arrived, who I heard it from, this was not anything that I ever spent much of my thoughts on. I never thought about this issue too much. I was troubled by many other things at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you think I'm accusing you of something and I'm not. I'm just trying to have you tell the Trial Chamber what I think is the case, and that is that matters that were going on in Omarska were generally known throughout the inmate population at Omarska rather quickly after they occurred because of the grapevine, because of the way news travelled in Omarska. That's all I'm asking. I'm not asking you to remember any of the things you heard or anything else. Just to agree with me and advise the Chamber that that was the case, and it was, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: What kind of news?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, like when the journalists visited. I mean that was something that everybody in Omarska learned rather quickly after their visit, right?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, probably that piece of news probably spread very quickly. After three months of torture and killing, finally somebody arrived to see what was going on, so it's very probable, it's very likely, that that piece of news did spread but I don't remember. It had to spread very quickly because it was an event. It was that straw that a man could cling to in order to survive, hope, "now they know we are here, they are killing us, they can see what we look like, we are hungry, tortured, full of lice in a terrible state, beaten, half dead."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You were not answering the question. The question was a very simple one. You seem to be worrying about the question when you don't need to worry about it. What you are being asked is a very simple question. In the environment you were in in this camp, is it correct, is it true, that news spread fast and around?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is a very simple question. Answer yes or no. I mean what difference is it going to make?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I make --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's all I want him to do. I think he is answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's like in a small village, if something happens, everyone knows about it within minutes. Was it like that in the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation in the camp was like this: We were placed in the different rooms and sometimes it would happen that a person would go to an interrogation from one room but then would be brought back to another room so that's when the information would spread. Sometimes ten or 20 days would pass and nobody would come to that room, and so on. So I cannot say that information spread quickly. Sometimes it did and sometimes it did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Your question now, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your testimony in the Stakic case, sir, you were talking about being, as you talked about earlier today, in that room with around 150 other men in that garage. And you said something in the Stakic case that was very interesting. I want to remind you of it and then ask you some questions about it. You said and I'm quoting and this is page 6357, "And then a jerry can filled with water was brought to us and then people started fighting over the jerry can. It was awful. It was a fight to survive as simple as that. No one really cared about the person next to them. We fought like animals over the water they had brought us. It was really awful." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned something about people at that moment, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned how human beings will behave when confronted with the fear of death.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's not what you would have expected before that moment, was it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was something that would not have occurred to me, not even in my dreams.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about the two men who died of suffocation and were just lying there on the floor and no one paying any attention to them. How could that be?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That nobody cared for those people?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, how could that be? How did that happen? How can you explain that change in behaviour that you observed there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know if that's something that can be explained at all. For me that's incomprehensible. Maybe it's some kind of survival instinct that takes over control, takes control over a man at times like that. Maybe some experts could explain that. I could not get to a better explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it that you all didn't sit around and talk about it and decide to behave that way, that it was just something that just happened, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whatever role you played in that was not something you decided to do but just something that came from somewhere inside you and inside the rest of those men?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Could you please explain or clarify your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you've probably already answered it. I'm just asking it in a different way. What you observed, what you yourself did during those moments, like when you talked about going outside and just ignoring a dead man lying there in front of you, about it not having any effect on you, that wasn't something that you consciously at some point decided to do but something that just happened because of some instinct or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown P1134, please? Could I be shown the English part of it before you take it to the witness? I just want to show you what part to put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you have a document before you that is Prosecution's Exhibit 1134. It's a report that was written by a commission that visited Omarska. You probably saw them there since you were probably there at the time. If you find the section, you'll have to turn a few pages and find the section in there that refers to Omarska, it's paragraph 2, "Omarska near Prijedor," it says. And if you look down to about the third paragraph, it starts with, "The prisoners." "The prisoners are kept in a hall containing military camp beds and orderly toilet facilities. Food is provided for them in the workers' canteen. The food is prepared in the mine's central building as provided on a self-service basis. A first aid point is located in one of the offices and is staffed by a physician and a nurse to administer any first aid that may be required, while in more serious cases, the prisoners are transferred to the medical centres in Banja Luka and Prijedor." I'll ask you firstly two questions. Does that fairly describe your experience in Omarska after the -- there were the 150 or so of you left there? And if not, what about it is not correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That was more or less the situation once we were left behind.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During all the time that were you in Omarska, you never saw or heard about any politicians visiting Omarska, did you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave a statement, do you remember giving a statement in Zenica on 22 February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's -- this was given to the Centre Institute for Investigation of Crimes against Humanity and International Law, Prijedor Municipality. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you want to look at this statement when I ask you questions about it, you can have a copy so just let me know if you want to see a copy, okay?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to read you what the statement indicates you said with regard to the situation where there was an attack upon Kozarac that we talked about a little bit earlier. What you said in this statement was, "As the enemy was numerous and better-armed --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be running out of tape in a few minutes -- we will be running out of tape in four minutes so we need to stop for a couple of minutes until they change the tape, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We can stop, Your Honour, if you want to take a -- let's see, I've probably got ten, 15 more minutes, if you want to stop right now and wait for them to go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With me it's no problem but I want to make sure that it's all right with the interpreters and the technicians. Because we have gone beyond the 25 minutes that you had mentioned. Okay. We stop for four minutes, we stay here, until they change the tape, and then we resume. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ackerman. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, we were talking about there statement that you gave in Zenica. "As the enemy was numerous and better armed, we did not succeed in preventing a breakthrough by their forces into our village." Whether you say, "We did not succeed in preventing a breakthrough," I assume that included you.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No. It does not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when you're giving a statement and using the term "we," you do not include yourself in that term "we"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, I don't include myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "We withdrew into the interior of what was then the free territory and took up positions." Were you part of that "we"?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you say "took up positions," did you dig trenches or what kind of positions did you take up?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I used the plural there. I explained who was at the checkpoint, who was in the basement, who was withdrawing. I used the plural saying, "We were withdrawing." There were people who were on the checkpoints but there were also women and children but we all withdrew. We were not all at the checkpoint. Some people withdrew to Kamicani, Brdjani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you write this statement yourself? Is it in your own handwriting?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I don't remember whose handwriting that was. If I may see the document, then I can confirm the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor show the witness this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Do you need an extra copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: To be given to the witness. The one I have is typical. It's copied in such a way that it can't be read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The question, since you have it before you is: Is that your handwriting or did someone else write that out?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: This is not my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at the last page and tell me if you see your signature there.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
