utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And right above your signature, you should see the language, "I affix my signature to confirm that everything contained in the above statement is true. And that I am prepared to give testimony before any court." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of this group that was withdrawing and taking up positions in the woods? Who was in charge of the group?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, misstates the evidence. He hasn't identified any group that was withdrawing and taking up positions in the woods. It's the second part I object to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your statement says "we withdrew into the interior of what was then the free territory and took up positions." Who was the commander of the "we" that withdrew into the interior into the free territory and took up positions. Who was in charge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you need to ask him first whether there was someone in charge.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody was in command. Simply, people were fleeing. We fled the village. Nobody ordered anybody, "You have to go there or you should go there." So nobody was in command. Yes, my father told me, "You are coming with me," and with my mother. We were going to the parents of my sister-in-law. Yes, and that's where we went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about this group of men that eventually was captured and put in Benkovac barracks that had weapons and some had uniforms, and when you say, "We withdrew into the interior of what was then the free territory and took up positions," what I'm trying to find out is did somebody give you directions as to which way to go and where to take up positions? Was somebody giving directions, saying, "Follow me, let's go here, come on, boys, bring your guns," or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The word was that we had to escape from the village and that we were to go towards Kamicani and towards Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: And that group, it was the people from around there, neighbours, cousins, women, children. Everybody who happened to be in the village on that day. We all withdrew from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this same statement in Zenica, the one you affixed your signature to confirm that everything contained in it was true, you said, "530 of us were transferred to Batkovici camp in a village near Bijeljina." That's what you said then, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I gave the statement. I said that I had given the statement. Now --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Then you gave a statement to the Prosecutor later on 11 January of 1996. In that statement you said, "I was transferred to Batkovici, a village close to Bijeljina together with approximately 500 prisoners." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. But right now I cannot remember how many of us were transferred. We were transferred to Batkovici, though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then there came a time in October of 2001 when an officer came from the Tribunal and showed you your statement and asked you -- you were asked if you wanted to make any corrections to and then you swore to the truth of your statement, and one of the corrections you made was that on page 4 of your statement, where you said that you went to Batkovici with 500 people, that should be reduced to 150 people, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After a period of time, you were exchanged, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. That is so. I was exchanged in September or October, 1993. I'm not sure about the exact date, whether it was the 10th of September or the 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that exchange, you joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No, not immediately. It was three or four months later that I joined the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did join the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And what did you do in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were you engaged in any fighting of any kind?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you left, then, after about four months after joining the army, you say that you fled to Croatia, true?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you desert the army? Were you discharged? How did you happen to leave the army?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I fled. I deserted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever faced any consequences as a result of that desertion?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. Relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: What is the relevance of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the relevance, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: There probably isn't any, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's giving evidence in open session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke about -- you spoke about this room you were in at Omarska and you said it was the garage with the 150 people. The words you used were this. You said it was like a gas chamber. You remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Gas chamber, yes, possibly, I don't remember. I can't remember every single word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was just today. Can you remember what you said today? Today you said it was like a gas chamber.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: I said it today?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Today, last time? I guess I did say that. Because that is how it was. That is what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Gas chamber is like? What kind of a gas chamber are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: A good question. I don't know. A very -- the air very closed, stuffy, nothing to breathe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Koumjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Re-examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you used the term gas chamber, you said it was difficult to breathe. How difficult was it to breathe in that room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: It was very -- the air was very close. I mean we were simply suffocating. We were gasping for breath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyone in the room become sick during the ten days that you were there?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: As I have already said, two persons died.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any one get intestinal problems? Did people have diarrhoea in the room?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: This goes beyond my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we don't need to go into all this, Mr. Koumjian. I think he's given already quite a vivid description of what it was like in there. I don't think we need more details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman asked you about the 80 armed men, I believe -- I don't want to misquote him, the group, the armed group of 80 people that you were captured with and then on the mountain. Were those all 80 people, were they all men?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe that group of people. You said there were four or five men in uniforms, some had guns, some other men had guns. What were the rest of the people like?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: They all looked like ordinary people. What do you mean? How could they have looked?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they men, were they women? What were their ages?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: The majority were men, and there were several women and some children. There were also some underage, some minors.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before being imprisoned in Omarska, did you own a gun?

utterances.speaker: SAMIR POLJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So Mr. Poljak, that brings us to the end of your testimony. I wish to thank you for having come again to this Tribunal to give evidence. You will now be escorted by the usher and you will be attended to, to assist you in your return to your country. Thank you once more.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Ms. Sutherland or Mr. Koumjian, tomorrow we are hearing the testimony of -- I just want the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, the first witness will be witness 7.79.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay and that is open session, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You expect that to last -- your in chief to last how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Ms. Korner is leading the witness. She has advised that she doesn't think it will take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And the witness which follows is Witness 7.226, and he has been granted protective measures, pseudonym, image and voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And you expect that to go into Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour, with cross-examination as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who will be examining --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You. And you expect your in chief to last how long?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Another estimate but perhaps three-quarters of an hour, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And he is witness BT-27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All right. So I would like to openly thank the interpreters and the technicians and the rest of the staff in this courtroom for their cooperation, which I can assure you we very much appreciate. I thank you once more. We will all meet tomorrow in the afternoon. It's tomorrow in the afternoon, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
